citations.sentence: Paul's letter context: teachers urging law-keeping; justification by faith in Christ; restoring someone caught in sin gently; the law of Christ as the way of Jesus.
citations.note: Scripture context paraphrased (Galatians overall, 6:1). Only Galatians 6:2 is quoted, byte-for-byte from verse.json chosen.text (curly apostrophe).

citations.sentence: Ligonier Ministries ... is testing an AI assistant that answers faith questions from its own teaching library. Its chief executive says it will 'defer to a real human' when users push past its limits.
The tool, Ask Ligonier, is in a limited beta, mainly for Ligonier's Ministry Partners, with a 30-day trial offered through the Grow app.
citations.note: Dossier safe wording.

citations.sentence: Peter D'Abrosca of Fox News Digital reported on the tool on Oct 31, with on-record comments from Ligonier president and CEO Chris Larson.
Fox calls the app 'Grow' and describes an 'intelligent answer assistant' inside it.
Ligonier Labs names that assistant Ask Ligonier. It says the assistant responds 'to questions about the Bible, theology, and the Christian life'.
Ligonier Labs says access to its experiments 'is limited to select users during their testing phase'.
The Ask Ligonier page calls the tool 'in-development' and says access 'is currently limited to Ministry Partners during this beta phase'.
Grow's App Store notes for version 12.0.1 (Sept 17) say 'This feature is available to Ministry Partners'.
citations.note: 'first appearing' dropped per factcheck.json (earlier versions not checked).

citations.sentence: The Grow website offers '30 free days of Ask Ligonier'.
'It is just trained on our library,' Larson told Fox.

He described '50 years of teaching' from 'more than 800 different teachers,' which he said is 'grounded in Dr. R.C. Sproul's lifetime of teaching.' Fox puts the library at 'tens of thousands of pieces of content'.
citations.note: Sproul wording now quoted and attributed to Larson per editor advisory.

citations.sentence: Ligonier's own page describes the assistant as 'drawing answers from Ligonier’s deep teaching library'.
Ligonier has not published which AI model runs underneath, or whether the system was trained on the library or simply looks answers up in it.
citations.note: Dossier 'Unverified / gaps'. Absence statement.

citations.sentence: He said Ligonier has 'given it a sandbox to work within.' He added that 'any time that somebody tries to push it beyond the borders, we're going to deflect or defer to a real human'.
citations.note: Split into the two fragments factcheck.json confirmed; leading 'And so' and joining wording removed.

citations.sentence: A sandbox, in software, is a fenced-off space where a program can act only within set rules.
citations.note: Term definition per style guide.

citations.sentence: If a user discusses suicidality, Fox reports, the assistant directs them to 'the suicide hotline'.
citations.note: Unconfirmed tail 'or other real-world resources' cut per factcheck.json.

citations.sentence: Larson said the assistant is 'not trying to pretend it's a person.' ... 'We don't want it to take the place of a pastor or a local church elder or even a parent'.
Anyone building AI tools, he said, 'needs to think through ethical guidelines'.
In 2018, Ligonier launched a chat service called Ask Ligonier that was 'staffed by a well-trained team' of people.
Ligonier has not said whether that team still operates or receives today's handoffs.
citations.note: Dossier gap. Absence statement.

citations.sentence: Barna Group asked Christians and pastors when an AI should pass a conversation to a person, in research released Oct 22 with partner Gloo.
For mentions of suicide or self-harm, 94% of pastors and 63% of practicing Christians said AI should connect the person to a human right away.
The widest gap was on spiritual crisis. There, 71% of pastors wanted an immediate handoff, compared with 32% of practicing Christians, and 23% of practicing Christians said AI can continue.
citations.note: f23 descriptor phrase cut (not verified verbatim by factcheck.json).

citations.sentence: Barna surveyed 1,514 adults, 683 of them practicing Christians, in November 2025, and 442 Protestant pastors in December 2025.
citations.note: 'U.S.' omitted (no geography).

citations.sentence: A theology assistant is a likely place for conversations about doubt to land.
citations.note: Analysis drawn from dossier section 4; softened per editor advisory.

citations.sentence: Barna also reported on Oct 6 that 79% of pastors say their church has neither a formal AI policy nor informal guidance.
Only 10% feel positive about AI providing spiritual counseling.
Every guardrail described here comes from Larson, through Fox. We found no outside test or review of Ask Ligonier.
citations.note: Dossier section 5. Absence statement.

citations.sentence: 'The human handoff only works if there's someone to hand off to,' said Barna's Daniel Copeland.
citations.note: Straight apostrophe used in prose; source uses curly.

citations.sentence: Barna notes that AI tools have usually offered 'a referral, not a connection'.
Ligonier has not said who the 'real human' is, or whether a handoff connects someone live.
citations.note: Dossier gap. Absence statement.

citations.sentence: Ligonier invites users to 'share your feedback directly within the experiment'.
We found no date for wider access.
citations.note: Dossier section 6. Absence statement.

citations.sentence: Barna surveyed 1,500 teens ages 13 to 18 in February, with Christ In Youth.
citations.note: 'U.S.' omitted.

citations.sentence: Among its 'Faith-Activated' teens, 46% strongly agree AI feels like a safe place for questions they wouldn't ask out loud, versus 28% of all teens.
citations.note: Now the lead finding per editor fix #3.

citations.sentence: Parents still come first: teens said they would feel most comfortable asking mom (84%) and dad (78%) for advice, with AI at 35%.
citations.note: Demoted to context per editor fix #3.

citations.sentence: Richard Hamilton: 'Our job is to make sure a trusted adult, not an algorithm, is in that space'.
The team behind the Bible app Blessed, which it says has more than 10 million users, built the Elah Ring S1.
citations.note: User count attributed as self-reported.

citations.sentence: The company says its Cross-Light and a gentle vibration provide a screen-free interaction.
citations.note: Checked wording only (editor round 2); stress-sensing claim removed.

citations.sentence: FaithMate is 'not a replacement for a pastor, prayer, Scripture, church, or meaningful relationships'.
This is a company release distributed through HackerNoon's Business Blogging Program, and we found no independent coverage.
citations.note: 'paid' removed (inference). 'No independent coverage' kept: dossier reports none found in research.

citations.sentence: A ministry-trained assistant can sound authoritative and still be mistaken ... someone in crisis who might confide in it instead of a pastor.
citations.note: topics.json wisdomConcern framing; no factual claim.

citations.sentence: In January, researchers studying other Bible chatbots, not Ask Ligonier, found they 'regularly framed one interpretive approach as definitive'.
citations.note: Dated January; explicitly not a test of Ligonier. 'Bible Society' and 'popular' cut (not visible to fact-checker).

citations.sentence: Dr Jonas Kurlberg warned that AI answers 'are often assumed to be neutral or factual,' so people question them less.
Dr Zoltán Schwáb asked whether 'wrestling with the biblical text is often more important than receiving the answer to your question'.
Proverbs says that 'in the multitude of counselors there is victory' (Proverbs 11:14, World English Bible).
citations.note: Translation labeled per factcheck.json. Exact substring of verse.json candidate text (Proverbs 11:14, WEB, bible-api.com).
